subject: biology

items.q: Carbon forms an enormous diversity of compounds, on which life is based. Which statement about the bonding of a single carbon atom is correct?
items.correct: It forms up to four covalent bonds, single or double, with carbon or other non-metal atoms
items.misconception: It forms any number of covalent bonds, which is why so many carbon compounds exist
items.why: Students hear that carbon forms "many bonds" and "millions of compounds" and merge the two ideas, so the number of bonds per atom is inflated to explain the number of compounds. A carbon atom has four outer electrons and forms a maximum of four covalent bonds. The diversity comes not from the number of bonds per atom but from the way carbon atoms can link to each other repeatedly, with single or double bonds, into unbranched chains, branched chains and single or multiple rings.
items.specStatementText: Why carbon can build so many different molecules
items.random_wrong: It transfers its four outer electrons to other atoms, giving charged compounds

items.q: A student measures the diameter of a cell as 7 µm. What is this diameter in nanometres?
items.correct: 7000 nm, because one micrometre is 1000 nanometres
items.misconception: 70 nm, because each prefix is ten times the next
items.why: The first two prefixes students meet, centi and milli, really are a factor of ten apart (1 cm = 10 mm), and the list kilo–centi–milli–micro–nano is learned as a sequence, so students assume the same step applies all the way down. The prefixes are not evenly spaced: centi is 10⁻², milli 10⁻³, micro 10⁻⁶ and nano 10⁻⁹. So 1 mm = 1000 µm and 1 µm = 1000 nm, but 1 cm = 10 mm. Each conversion must use the actual power of ten of each prefix.
items.specStatementText: Why carbon can build so many different molecules
items.random_wrong: 0.007 nm, because a smaller unit means a smaller number

items.q: Which statement about the SI prefixes kilo, centi, milli, micro and nano is correct?
items.correct: Their meanings are conventions fixed by international agreement
items.misconception: Their meanings were discovered by scientists measuring natural objects
items.why: Scientific knowledge is presented to students as discovered truth, and they do not distinguish the facts science discovers from the conventions scientists agree in order to communicate those facts. SI prefixes and units are conventions: they are agreed internationally so that measurements are unambiguous, and they could in principle have been defined differently. The nature of science includes recognizing which parts of science are conventions rather than discoveries.
items.specStatementText: Why carbon can build so many different molecules
items.random_wrong: Each prefix is one tenth of the prefix that comes before it

items.q: Two monosaccharides are joined by a condensation reaction to form a disaccharide. What happens in this reaction?
items.correct: A covalent bond forms between the monomers and a molecule of water is released
items.misconception: A molecule of water is taken in and split to supply the atoms that join the monomers
items.why: The two reactions are taught together as a pair and are the reverse of each other, so students remember that water is involved in both but swap which direction consumes it, often because "hydro-" makes them think water is being produced. Condensation forms a bond and releases water (an -OH from one monomer and an -H from the other combine). Hydrolysis breaks a bond by adding water: the water molecule is split and its -H and -OH are incorporated into the products. The prefix hydro- and the ending -lysis mean "splitting with water".
items.specStatementText: Condensation joins monomers into polymers
items.random_wrong: A hydrogen bond forms between the two monomers, holding them together as a disaccharide

items.q: A polypeptide made of 100 amino acids is completely hydrolysed into free amino acids. How many water molecules are used in the process?
items.correct: 99 water molecules
items.misconception: 100 water molecules
items.why: Students learn "one condensation reaction joins one monomer and releases one water molecule" and count one reaction per monomer, forgetting that the first monomer needs no reaction to be part of the chain. Bonds lie between monomers, so a chain of n monomers has n − 1 bonds. Building it releases n − 1 water molecules and hydrolysing it completely uses n − 1, since each bond is made or broken by one water molecule.
items.specStatementText: Hydrolysis splits polymers back into monomers
items.random_wrong: 1 water molecule

items.q: Why is the digestion of a polymer into its monomers described as a hydrolysis reaction?
items.correct: Water molecules are split, and the -H and -OH produced are added to the monomers
items.misconception: Water acts only as the solvent in which enzymes break the polymer into its monomers
items.why: Water is the background to every reaction in a cell, so students treat it as inert. Digestion is taught as "enzymes break down large molecules", which leaves no visible role for water, and the equation is rarely written out with H₂O on the left. Hydrolysis means splitting with water. Breaking each bond between monomers consumes one water molecule, which is split to provide the -H and -OH groups incorporated into the monomers. Water is a reactant, not merely the medium.
items.specStatementText: Hydrolysis splits polymers back into monomers
items.random_wrong: Breaking the bonds between the monomers releases the energy that was stored in those bonds

items.q: Two monosaccharides, P and Q, are drawn in their ring forms. In P the ring is made of four carbon atoms and one oxygen atom, with one further carbon atom (in a CH₂OH group) attached outside the ring. In Q the ring is also made of four carbon atoms and one oxygen atom, but two further carbon atoms (each in a CH₂OH group) are attached outside the ring. How should P and Q be classified?
items.correct: P is a pentose and Q is a hexose
items.misconception: Both P and Q are pentose sugars
items.why: The two ring diagrams students see most, ribose (five-membered ring) and glucose (six-membered ring), happen to fit this rule, so it appears to work; students do not notice that one ring atom is oxygen and that carbon atoms also lie outside the ring. The names pentose and hexose refer to the number of carbon atoms in the molecule. In the ring form one ring atom is oxygen and at least one carbon lies outside the ring, so the ring size does not give the answer: fructose is a hexose although its ring has only five atoms.
items.specStatementText: Monosaccharides, and why glucose suits its job
items.random_wrong: Both P and Q are hexose sugars

items.q: Which statement correctly links a property of glucose to the way it is used in organisms?
items.correct: Glucose is chemically stable, so it is transported in blood plasma without breaking down
items.misconception: Glucose breaks down readily on its own, which is why it is used as a respiratory substrate
items.why: Students equate "energy-rich" with "reactive" and know that glucose is used up quickly in respiration, so they picture it as a fragile molecule that falls apart readily. Glucose is chemically stable: its covalent bonds do not break spontaneously, which is exactly what makes it safe to transport in the blood and to store as polymers. The energy yield comes from its oxidation in cell respiration, a controlled, enzyme-catalysed process.
items.specStatementText: Monosaccharides, and why glucose suits its job
items.random_wrong: Glucose dissolves in water because its molecules are small, so it is easily transported

items.q: Liver cells store glucose in the form of glycogen. Why is the glucose not simply stored as free glucose?
items.correct: Glycogen is relatively insoluble because of its size, so it does not affect the osmotic balance of the cell
items.misconception: Glycogen is insoluble because it is non-polar, so it stays separate from the watery cytoplasm
items.why: Students learn one explanation for insolubility, the hydrophobic nature of lipids, and apply it to any insoluble substance, without noticing that polysaccharides are built from a highly polar, soluble monomer. Starch and glycogen are polymers of glucose and are covered in polar hydroxyl groups, so they are not hydrophobic. Their relative insolubility is due to their large molecular size, which is why they can be stored in large amounts without osmotic effects.
items.specStatementText: Starch and glycogen store energy compactly
items.random_wrong: The branches of glycogen make its glucose hard to remove, so the store is not used up too quickly

items.q: In glycogen a branch occurs roughly every 10 glucose monomers; in the amylopectin of starch a branch occurs roughly every 25 monomers, and amylose is unbranched. Animals often need to release glucose from their stores very rapidly. Which explanation best accounts for the high degree of branching in glycogen?
items.correct: Monomers are removed by hydrolysis at chain ends, so more branches give more ends to act on at once
items.misconception: Branches shield the glycosidic bonds, slowing hydrolysis so that the store is released steadily over time
items.why: Students picture branches as making a structure more tangled and therefore more resistant to attack, and the idea of a store suggests something that should be locked away. The opposite is true. Hydrolysis (and condensation) happens at the ends of chains, and every branch creates an extra end, so a highly branched glycogen molecule can release glucose from many points at once. Branching also makes the molecule compact.
items.specStatementText: Starch and glycogen store energy compactly
items.random_wrong: Branching makes glycogen non-polar, so that it remains insoluble until the glucose is actually required

items.q: Amylose, a polymer of alpha-glucose, forms a coiled chain, whereas cellulose, a polymer of beta-glucose, forms a straight chain. Why does the cellulose chain not coil?
items.correct: Each beta-glucose is rotated 180° relative to its neighbours, so the chain is straight
items.misconception: Beta-glucose has a different molecular formula, and its extra atoms make the chain rigid
items.why: The two are given different names and build polymers with strikingly different properties (starch and cellulose), so students assume the monomers must differ substantially, and ring diagrams that are hard to read hide how small the difference is. Both are C₆H₁₂O₆ and are interconvertible in solution. The only difference is whether the -OH on carbon 1 is below or above the plane of the ring, yet this determines whether the resulting polymer coils (starch) or forms straight chains (cellulose).
items.specStatementText: Cellulose: straight chains bundled into a strong wall
items.random_wrong: Covalent bonds between neighbouring cellulose chains pull each chain out straight and flat

items.q: Cellulose gives plant cell walls high tensile strength. Which feature of cellulose is responsible for this?
items.correct: Straight chains lie side by side in bundles, cross-linked by many hydrogen bonds
items.misconception: The glycosidic bonds within cellulose are very much stronger than those within starch
items.why: Students associate strength with strong bonds, and covalent bonds are the strong bonds they know, so they assume a strong material must be covalently cross-linked. The glycosidic bonds in cellulose and starch are both covalent and of similar strength. The tensile strength of cellulose comes from its straight chains lying side by side in bundles, held by a very large number of hydrogen bonds: each is weak, but together they resist stretching.
items.specStatementText: Cellulose: straight chains bundled into a strong wall
items.random_wrong: The chains coil into tight helices that stretch and recoil like a spring

items.q: The ABO blood groups depend on glycoproteins on the surface of red blood cells. Which statement about these ABO antigens is correct?
items.correct: The A and B antigens differ only in the sugar at the end of their carbohydrate chain
items.misconception: The A and B antigens are two entirely different proteins with unrelated amino acid sequences
items.why: Antigens are usually introduced as proteins on the surface of pathogens, and the ABO groups are inherited, so students assume each allele codes directly for a different antigen protein. ABO antigens are glycoproteins whose identity depends on the carbohydrate, not the protein. The alleles of the ABO gene encode enzymes that add different terminal sugars to a shared base chain, so the A and B antigens differ only in that final sugar, and the immune system recognizes that difference.
items.specStatementText: Glycoproteins let cells recognize each other
items.random_wrong: Group O red blood cells carry a third antigen, the O antigen, in the place of the A or B

items.q: A triglyceride is only sparingly soluble in water but dissolves readily in a non-polar solvent. What explains this?
items.correct: Its molecules are mostly non-polar C–H bonds, with few groups that hydrogen-bond to water
items.misconception: Its molecules are too large to fit between water molecules, but a non-polar solvent has more room
items.why: Large size is the explanation given for the insolubility of starch and glycogen, so students reuse it for lipids, which are also described as macromolecules. Size is not the reason: a triglyceride is much smaller than a soluble protein such as haemoglobin, and a molecule of testosterone is smaller than a molecule of sucrose. Lipids are hydrophobic because they are non-polar. They dissolve in non-polar solvents, whose molecules interact with them by the same weak attractions.
items.specStatementText: Lipids are defined by what they dissolve in
items.random_wrong: Its molecules are less dense than water, so they float on the surface rather than dissolving

items.q: Which components are linked together by condensation reactions to form one phospholipid molecule?
items.correct: One glycerol, two fatty acids and one phosphate group
items.misconception: One glycerol, three fatty acids and one phosphate group
items.why: Phospholipids are introduced immediately after triglycerides and described as "similar to a triglyceride but with a phosphate group", which students read as an addition rather than a replacement. Glycerol has only three hydroxyl groups, so it can link only three components. In a phospholipid the phosphate group takes the place of one of the fatty acids: the molecule has two fatty acid tails and one phosphate head.
items.specStatementText: Triglycerides and phospholipids are built by condensation
items.random_wrong: Three glycerol molecules, one fatty acid and one phosphate group

items.q: One glycerol molecule and three fatty acid molecules react by condensation to form one triglyceride. How much water is produced?
items.correct: Three water molecules are released
items.misconception: One water molecule is released
items.why: The word equation "polymer + water → monomers" is written as one line, and students take it to describe one reaction rather than a summary of many. Each hydrolysis reaction breaks one bond and uses one water molecule. Complete digestion of a polymer is a series of such reactions, one per bond, so the number of water molecules used equals the number of bonds broken.
items.specStatementText: Triglycerides and phospholipids are built by condensation
items.random_wrong: Four water molecules are released

items.q: Three fatty acids each have 18 carbon atoms in their chain. X has no C=C double bonds, Y has one and Z has three. Which has the lowest melting point, and why?
items.correct: Z, because its C=C bonds kink the chain so that molecules pack less closely together
items.misconception: X, because C=C bonds are stronger than single bonds and hold Y and Z molecules together
items.why: Students know that a double bond is stronger than a single bond and assume that stronger bonds within a molecule mean a stronger, higher-melting substance, confusing bonds within molecules with attractions between molecules. Melting does not break covalent bonds; it overcomes the weak attractions between molecules. Kinked unsaturated chains pack less closely, so those attractions are weaker and the melting point is lower, which is why oils rich in unsaturated fatty acids are liquid at room temperature.
items.specStatementText: Double bonds, melting point and where fats are stored
items.random_wrong: Z, because it has the fewest hydrogen atoms and so the fewest bonds to break as it melts

items.q: A student analysed two energy stores. Oil from a plant seed contained 12% saturated and 88% unsaturated fatty acids; fat from a mammal's adipose tissue contained 55% saturated and 45% unsaturated fatty acids. At 20°C the oil was liquid and the fat was solid. Which explanation best accounts for the difference?
items.correct: The mammal keeps a high, constant body temperature at which a store rich in saturated fatty acids stays fluid enough, while the seed is at lower environmental temperatures and needs unsaturated fatty acids with low melting points
items.misconception: The mammal's fat must be solid inside its body, so it requires the higher melting point that a high proportion of saturated fatty acids provides, whereas the seed's oil only needs to be liquid at room temperature
items.why: Fats and oils are defined by their state at about 20°C, and that is the only temperature at which students ever see them, so room temperature becomes the reference point for storage inside the body as well. The relevant temperature is the one at which the store is held. An endotherm keeps its body at a high, constant temperature, so fats with a higher proportion of saturated fatty acids stay sufficiently fluid inside it even though they are solid at room temperature. A plant is at environmental temperature, often well below 20°C, so its stores are oils rich in unsaturated fatty acids.
items.specStatementText: Double bonds, melting point and where fats are stored
items.random_wrong: The mammal's fat is solid because saturated fatty acids contain many C=C double bonds, which raise the melting point, whereas the unsaturated fatty acids of the oil have none and so remain liquid

items.q: Which property of triglycerides makes them well suited to long-term energy storage in adipose tissue?
items.correct: They release about twice the energy per gram of carbohydrates when oxidized
items.misconception: They release less energy per gram than carbohydrates, so a store of them lasts longer
items.why: Sports and diet advice presents carbohydrate as "the energy food" because it is mobilized quickly, and students turn speed of release into amount of energy. Per gram, triglycerides release about twice as much energy as carbohydrates, and they are stored without the water that accompanies glycogen, so they are the compact long-term store. Glycogen is used for shorter-term storage because glucose can be released from it rapidly.
items.specStatementText: Adipose tissue: energy store and insulator
items.random_wrong: They are very large molecules, so they cannot dissolve and leave the adipose cell

items.q: A seal living in polar seas has a layer of adipose tissue (blubber) several centimetres thick beneath its skin. A dolphin of similar size living in tropical seas has a much thinner layer, and a cod living in the same polar seas as the seal has very little adipose tissue beneath its skin. Which explanation accounts for all three observations?
items.correct: Adipose tissue slows heat loss, so an endotherm needs more of it the larger the gap between its body and habitat temperatures, and the cod's body is at almost the temperature of the water
items.misconception: All animals in cold water need thick insulation, so the cod must have an equally thick layer of fat elsewhere in its body to keep itself warm in the polar sea
items.why: Insulation is taught with examples such as seals, whales and polar bears, and students generalize from "cold habitat" without considering whether the animal generates and maintains its own body heat. Insulation only slows heat flow from a warmer body to colder surroundings. An ectotherm in cold water is at almost the same temperature as the water, so a fat layer would retain no heat; only endotherms, whose body temperature is well above the habitat temperature, benefit from thick blubber.
items.specStatementText: Adipose tissue: energy store and insulator
items.random_wrong: Blubber generates the heat that keeps the seal warm in polar water, the dolphin needs to generate less heat in warm water, and the cod does not generate any heat at all

items.q: Phospholipids are shaken with water in a test tube, with no cells or enzymes present. What happens, and why?
items.correct: Bilayers form, because the hydrophilic heads face the water and the hydrophobic tails face each other
items.misconception: Nothing organized forms, because phospholipid bilayers can only be built by enzymes inside living cells
items.why: Almost every structure students meet in biology is made by cellular machinery, so self-assembly driven only by the properties of the molecules and of water is unfamiliar. Bilayer formation is a consequence of the hydrophobic and hydrophilic regions of the phospholipid, not of enzyme action. Phospholipids shaken with water form bilayers and vesicles on their own; cells make the phospholipids, but the bilayer assembles itself.
items.specStatementText: Phospholipids arrange themselves into bilayers
items.random_wrong: Bilayers form, because covalent bonds link the fatty acid tails of neighbouring phospholipids

items.q: Testosterone binds to receptors inside its target cells. How does it get through the plasma membrane to reach them?
items.correct: It is a non-polar steroid, so it dissolves in the hydrophobic core of the bilayer and diffuses across
items.misconception: It is too large to pass between the phospholipids, so it is carried through a channel protein
items.why: Membrane transport is taught with the rule that only small molecules pass through the bilayer, and hormones are thought of as large signalling molecules that act at receptors on the surface. What decides whether a molecule can cross the bilayer directly is mainly its polarity, not just its size. Steroids are non-polar, so they dissolve in the hydrophobic interior of the membrane and pass through by simple diffusion, reaching receptors inside the cell.
items.specStatementText: Steroids slip through the bilayer
items.random_wrong: It is a protein hormone, so it is pulled into the cell after binding to a receptor on the surface

items.q: Four molecules are drawn as molecular diagrams. Which description identifies the molecule that is a steroid?
items.correct: Four fused rings of carbon atoms, three with six atoms and one with five
items.misconception: A single six-membered ring made up of five carbon atoms and one oxygen atom
items.why: Steroids are the molecules whose ring structure students are asked to recognize, so "ring" becomes the identifying feature, even though monosaccharides and nucleotide bases are also drawn as rings. A single ring is not diagnostic: glucose and ribose are drawn as rings. A steroid is identified by its four fused rings sharing edges, three with six atoms and one with five, and the molecule is a non-polar lipid rather than a sugar.
items.specStatementText: Steroids slip through the bilayer
items.random_wrong: A chain of amino acids folded up into a compact globular shape

items.q: What is a covalent bond?
items.correct: A bond in which two atoms share a pair of electrons, each contributing one electron to the shared pair.
items.misconception: A covalent bond forms when one atom gives its outer electrons to another, so bonded atoms carry charges.
items.why: GCSE and MYP chemistry usually teach ionic bonding first, with vivid diagrams of electrons being transferred, and students carry the idea of transfer over to every bond they meet later. Electrons are transferred only in ionic bonding. In a covalent bond the two atoms share a pair of electrons and stay neutral, which is why carbon compounds are uncharged, stable molecules held together by strong bonds.
items.specStatementText: Why carbon can build so many different molecules
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What kind of bond holds the monomers of a polymer together?
items.correct: A covalent bond, formed by a condensation reaction: a glycosidic bond in polysaccharides, a peptide bond in polypeptides and a bond between phosphate and sugar in nucleic acids.
items.misconception: Monomers are held together in a polymer by hydrogen bonds or other weak attractions, so polymers come apart easily.
items.why: Hydrogen bonds are the bonds students hear most about in biology (in water, DNA base pairing and protein folding), and diagrams of polymers show monomers as beads touching one another, so the joining bond is imagined as a weak attraction. The bond formed in a condensation reaction is a strong covalent bond, which is why polymers are stable and need enzyme-catalysed hydrolysis to break them. Hydrogen bonds act between molecules or between different parts of a large molecule, not as the link between consecutive monomers.
items.specStatementText: Condensation joins monomers into polymers
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a triglyceride a polymer?
items.correct: No. A triglyceride is a large molecule made from a fixed set of four components (one glycerol and three fatty acids), not a chain of repeating monomers, so it is not a polymer.
items.misconception: Triglycerides and other lipids are polymers, made from fatty acid monomers in the same way that starch is made from glucose.
items.why: Lipids are taught alongside carbohydrates, proteins and nucleic acids as one of the four groups of "biological molecules", and the other three are all polymers formed by condensation, so students assume lipids follow the same monomer-to-polymer pattern. Condensation reactions do form triglycerides, but they link one glycerol to three fatty acids, giving a molecule with a fixed structure rather than a chain of repeated monomers. Polysaccharides, polypeptides and nucleic acids are polymers; triglycerides are macromolecular lipids, not polymers.
items.specStatementText: Triglycerides and phospholipids are built by condensation
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is energy released when the bonds between monomers in a polymer are broken?
items.correct: No. Breaking a bond requires an input of energy; hydrolysis of polymers during digestion releases very little energy. The large energy yield comes later, when monomers such as glucose are oxidized in cell respiration.
items.misconception: Energy is stored in the bonds between monomers, so breaking those bonds during digestion releases the energy stored in the food.
items.why: Everyday phrases such as "energy-rich bonds" and "food contains energy", together with the description of ATP as releasing energy when its bond is broken, lead students to believe that bond-breaking itself releases energy. Bond breaking always absorbs energy; energy is released when new, more stable bonds form. Digestion by hydrolysis only breaks polymers into monomers; the energy from food is released when those monomers are oxidized in cell respiration, forming carbon dioxide and water.
items.specStatementText: Hydrolysis splits polymers back into monomers
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why does glucose dissolve in water?
items.correct: Because its many polar hydroxyl (-OH) groups form hydrogen bonds with water molecules.
items.misconception: Glucose dissolves because it is a small molecule; small molecules dissolve and large ones do not.
items.why: Students learn that polysaccharides are insoluble because they are large and then apply size as the only rule for solubility, and glucose is indeed small. Solubility depends on polarity, not size alone. Glucose is soluble because its hydroxyl groups hydrogen-bond with water; a fatty acid or a steroid is also small but is only sparingly soluble because it is non-polar. Size matters for polysaccharides only because it makes hydrogen bonding with water insufficient to pull the giant molecule into solution.
items.specStatementText: Monosaccharides, and why glucose suits its job
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In what form do cells store glucose for later use?
items.correct: As a polysaccharide (glycogen in animals, starch in plants), not as free glucose.
items.misconception: Cells can store energy simply by keeping a large amount of glucose dissolved in the cytoplasm, since glucose is so soluble.
items.why: Solubility is presented as a useful property of glucose, so students see no reason not to store it dissolved; the osmotic consequences of a high solute concentration are not obvious. A high concentration of dissolved glucose would draw water into the cell by osmosis and could disturb its metabolism. Cells convert glucose by condensation into compact, relatively insoluble polysaccharides that have no osmotic effect and can be mobilized by hydrolysis when needed.
items.specStatementText: Starch and glycogen store energy compactly
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What shape does a cellulose molecule have?
items.correct: A straight, unbranched chain, because successive beta-glucose monomers alternate in orientation.
items.misconception: Cellulose molecules are coiled or branched like starch, and it is the coiling or branching that makes them strong.
items.why: Cellulose and starch are both polymers of glucose and are learned together, so the coiled and branched shapes drawn for starch are transferred to cellulose. Cellulose chains are straight and unbranched: each beta-glucose is rotated 180° relative to the next, which prevents coiling. Straight chains can pack side by side in bundles cross-linked by hydrogen bonds, and it is this arrangement, not coiling or branching, that gives cellulose its strength.
items.specStatementText: Cellulose: straight chains bundled into a strong wall
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which way does the carbohydrate part of a membrane glycoprotein face?
items.correct: Outwards, projecting from the outer surface of the plasma membrane into the surroundings of the cell.
items.misconception: The carbohydrate chains of glycoproteins face into the cytoplasm, or are found on both faces of the membrane.
items.why: Membrane diagrams show proteins spanning the bilayer symmetrically and are often drawn without indicating which side is outside, so the orientation of the carbohydrate is not registered. Carbohydrate chains are attached only on the extracellular face of the plasma membrane, where they can be contacted by other cells and by antibodies. This is what makes glycoproteins the basis of cell–cell recognition.
items.specStatementText: Glycoproteins let cells recognize each other
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What antigen do the red blood cells of a person with blood group O carry?
items.correct: Neither the A antigen nor the B antigen: their cells carry only the unmodified base carbohydrate chain, so there is no "O antigen".
items.misconception: Group O cells carry an O antigen, just as group A cells carry an A antigen and group B cells a B antigen.
items.why: The naming of the groups A, B, AB and O suggests four antigens in parallel, and students extend the pattern from A and B to O. The letter O stands for the absence of both A and B antigens. Group O red cells carry the base chain to which the A or B sugar would be added, but no terminal A or B sugar, which is why group O blood provokes no anti-A or anti-B response in a recipient.
items.specStatementText: Glycoproteins let cells recognize each other
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why does oil float on water without mixing with it?
items.correct: It floats because it is less dense than water, but it does not mix because it is non-polar and cannot hydrogen-bond with water; the two properties are separate.
items.misconception: Oil does not mix with water because it is lighter than water, so it floats on top instead of dissolving.
items.why: The everyday observation of oil floating on water combines two things (floating and not mixing) into one, and density is the explanation students know for floating. Density determines whether a liquid floats, not whether it dissolves: ethanol is also less dense than water yet mixes with it completely. Lipids fail to dissolve because they are hydrophobic, consisting mostly of non-polar C–H bonds.
items.specStatementText: Lipids are defined by what they dissolve in
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which substances are classed as lipids?
items.correct: Any substance in living organisms that dissolves in non-polar solvents but is only sparingly soluble in water: fats, oils, waxes and steroids.
items.misconception: Lipids are the same thing as fats, so oils, waxes and steroids are not lipids.
items.why: In everyday language "fat" and "lipid" are used as synonyms, and diet advice talks only about fats and oils, so the wider class defined by solubility is unfamiliar. Lipids are defined by their solubility, not by one structure. Fats and oils are triglycerides, but waxes and steroids such as testosterone and oestradiol are also lipids, because they share the property of dissolving in non-polar solvents rather than in water.
items.specStatementText: Lipids are defined by what they dissolve in
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What are the components of a triglyceride?
items.correct: One glycerol molecule linked to three fatty acid molecules.
items.misconception: A triglyceride is made from three glycerol molecules and one fatty acid.
items.why: The prefix tri- is attached to the glycerol part of the name, so students read "tri-glyceride" as "three glycerols". The name refers to the three fatty acids that are attached to one glycerol. Glycerol has three hydroxyl groups, and each forms an ester bond with the carboxyl group of one fatty acid by a condensation reaction, so three fatty acids fit on one glycerol.
items.specStatementText: Triglycerides and phospholipids are built by condensation
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What does "saturated" mean when applied to a fatty acid?
items.correct: That the hydrocarbon chain has no C=C double bonds: every carbon atom is saturated with hydrogen, carrying as many hydrogen atoms as it can.
items.misconception: A saturated fatty acid is one that is full of double bonds.
items.why: "Saturated" in everyday use means "full of something", and double bonds are the feature students are told to look for, so they assume a saturated fatty acid is full of double bonds. A fatty acid is saturated with hydrogen, not with double bonds. A saturated fatty acid has only single C–C bonds; a monounsaturated one has one C=C and a polyunsaturated one has two or more.
items.specStatementText: Double bonds, melting point and where fats are stored
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the C=O bond in the carboxyl group count when deciding whether a fatty acid is unsaturated?
items.correct: No. Only carbon–carbon double bonds (C=C) in the hydrocarbon chain count; the C=O of the carboxyl group is present in every fatty acid.
items.misconception: Any double bond in a fatty acid makes it unsaturated, so the C=O bond in the -COOH group means every fatty acid is unsaturated.
items.why: Students are told to "look for double bonds" and the carboxyl group, drawn prominently at one end of every structure, contains an obvious one. Saturation refers to the hydrocarbon chain only. Every fatty acid has the C=O of its carboxyl group; what distinguishes saturated, monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids is the number of C=C bonds between carbon atoms in the chain.
items.specStatementText: Double bonds, melting point and where fats are stored
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How does a layer of adipose tissue keep an animal warm?
items.correct: It is a poor conductor of heat, so it slows the transfer of heat from the warm body to the colder surroundings.
items.misconception: Fat keeps an animal warm because it produces heat, or because it is itself warm.
items.why: Everyday phrases such as "a warm layer of fat" and the observation that well-insulated animals feel warm to the touch suggest that the fat is the source of the warmth. The insulating role of adipose tissue is to reduce the rate at which heat produced by metabolism is lost through the skin; the layer itself is not the source of that heat. This is why the layer is thickest in endotherms living where the difference between body and habitat temperature is greatest.
items.specStatementText: Adipose tissue: energy store and insulator
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What does "amphipathic" mean?
items.correct: Having both a hydrophilic region and a hydrophobic region in the same molecule, as a phospholipid has a hydrophilic phosphate head and hydrophobic fatty acid tails.
items.misconception: Amphipathic means that a molecule can act as both an acid and a base.
items.why: The word resembles "amphoteric", which students meet in chemistry with exactly that meaning, and the prefix amphi- ("both") does not say both of what. Amphipathic refers to the two contrasting regions of a molecule with respect to water: one part hydrophilic, the other hydrophobic. It has nothing to do with acid–base behaviour. This dual nature is what makes phospholipids assemble into bilayers.
items.specStatementText: Phospholipids arrange themselves into bilayers
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What holds the phospholipids of a bilayer together?
items.correct: The hydrophobic effect: the fatty acid tails are excluded from water and cluster together, while the hydrophilic heads associate with water. There are no covalent bonds between neighbouring phospholipids.
items.misconception: The phospholipids in a bilayer are joined to one another by covalent bonds, which is why the membrane holds together.
items.why: Membrane diagrams show phospholipids packed in a neat, regular array, and students assume that anything so orderly and stable must be bonded together. Neighbouring phospholipids are not covalently bonded. The bilayer forms and persists because the hydrophobic tails are excluded from water and the hydrophilic heads face it; because the attractions involved are weak, individual phospholipids can move, and the membrane is fluid as well as stable.
items.specStatementText: Phospholipids arrange themselves into bilayers
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What kind of molecule is testosterone?
items.correct: A steroid: a lipid built on four fused carbon rings.
items.misconception: Steroid hormones such as testosterone and oestradiol are proteins, like other hormones.
items.why: Hormones are introduced through examples such as insulin, which is a protein, and "anabolic steroids" are associated with building muscle protein, so students assume all hormones are proteins. Testosterone and oestradiol are steroids, which are lipids: their molecules consist of four fused rings of carbon atoms. Because they are non-polar lipids, unlike protein hormones, they can pass through the phospholipid bilayer and act on receptors inside the cell.
items.specStatementText: Steroids slip through the bilayer
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When 7 µm is converted into nanometres, should the number get larger or smaller?
items.correct: Larger: a nanometre is a smaller unit, so more of them are needed to make the same length (7 µm = 7000 nm).
items.misconception: Converting to a smaller unit such as nanometres makes the number smaller, because nano means tiny.
items.why: The word "smaller" is attached to the unit and gets transferred to the number, and students remember conversions as "divide by 1000" without checking the direction. The length does not change, only the unit. A smaller unit fits into the same length more times, so the number goes up: 7 µm = 7 × 1000 nm = 7000 nm. Converting the other way, to a larger unit, makes the number smaller.
items.specStatementText: Why carbon can build so many different molecules
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which is the larger unit, a millimetre or a micrometre?
items.correct: A millimetre: milli is 10⁻³ and micro is 10⁻⁶, so 1 mm = 1000 µm.
items.misconception: Micro means one thousandth and milli means one millionth (the two are swapped).
items.why: Both prefixes begin with m, both are written with an m-like symbol (m and µ), and both are met at about the same time when learning cell sizes, so the two are easily interchanged. Milli (m) is 10⁻³, one thousandth; micro (µ) is 10⁻⁶, one millionth. Cells are measured in micrometres precisely because they are much smaller than a millimetre.
items.specStatementText: Why carbon can build so many different molecules

items.q: Do all monosaccharides have six carbon atoms?
items.correct: No. Hexoses such as glucose have six, but pentoses such as ribose and deoxyribose have five.
items.misconception: Every monosaccharide has six carbon atoms, like glucose.
items.why: Glucose is by far the most frequently used example of a sugar, so its formula C₆H₁₂O₆ comes to stand for monosaccharides in general. Monosaccharides vary in carbon number. Pentoses (five carbons) include ribose and deoxyribose, the sugars of RNA and DNA; hexoses (six carbons) include glucose, fructose and galactose. The class is found by counting carbon atoms.
items.specStatementText: Monosaccharides, and why glucose suits its job
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How does a layer of blubber insulate a marine mammal?
items.correct: The adipose tissue itself is a poor conductor of heat, so it slows the loss of heat from the body to the water.
items.misconception: Fat insulates in the same way as fur or feathers, by trapping a layer of air against the skin.
items.why: Trapped air is the insulation mechanism taught for fur, feathers and clothing, so students transfer it to the other insulating layer they meet. Blubber contains no air. Triglyceride-filled adipose tissue is itself a poor conductor of heat, which is why it works under water, where a layer of trapped air would be lost.
items.specStatementText: Adipose tissue: energy store and insulator
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How does a steroid hormone enter its target cell?
items.correct: By simple diffusion through the phospholipid bilayer, because it is a non-polar lipid.
items.misconception: Steroid hormones are taken into the cell by endocytosis, enclosed in a vesicle.
items.why: Endocytosis is presented as the way large or complex substances enter cells, and hormones are thought of as complex molecules that must be taken in actively. A steroid needs no vesicle: being non-polar, it dissolves in the hydrophobic interior of the bilayer and diffuses straight through, then binds to a receptor inside the cell.
items.specStatementText: Steroids slip through the bilayer
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why does a saturated fatty acid have a higher melting point than an unsaturated one of the same chain length?
items.correct: Because its straight chains pack closely, so the attractions between molecules are stronger and more energy is needed to separate them. Melting overcomes these weak intermolecular attractions and breaks no covalent bonds.
items.misconception: Saturated fatty acids have more atoms (more hydrogen) and therefore more bonds, and more bonds need more heat to break, so they melt at a higher temperature.
items.why: Students learn that heating breaks bonds and that saturated chains carry more hydrogen, so they count the bonds in the molecule rather than thinking about how the chains pack against one another. When a fat melts the molecules stay intact; they simply gain enough energy to move apart from one another. Melting point therefore depends on how strongly molecules attract one another, which for fatty acids depends on how closely their chains can pack, not on how many bonds each molecule contains.
